analysis.one_liner: Stops leasing low-value federal land for speculative oil and gas, requiring proof of development potential first.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee in May 2023 and received no hearing, markup, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the government from offering federal land for oil and gas leases when analysis shows the land has low or no potential to produce oil or gas. Today, companies can snap up these cheap leases mostly for speculation, which ties up public land used for grazing, recreation, and wildlife, and brings taxpayers almost no revenue. Under the bill, the Bureau of Land Management would have to assess each acre's potential, invite public comment, and could still lease land near producing wells to protect existing operators.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently get minimal revenue from leases on land that rarely produces oil or gas; recreationists, ranchers, and wildlife, whose uses of public land can be blocked by speculative leases that sit unused; and responsible oil and gas producers, who no longer compete with speculators hoarding cheap acreage.

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids offering land for lease if the government's own development analysis designates it as having low or no oil and gas potential, ending a practice the bill's findings say regularly leases land 'known or believed' to be worth little, for near-minimum bids, with minimal revenue to taxpayers [S2][S3].

Before leasing any land not covered by a current development analysis, the Bureau of Land Management would have to complete one that grades every acre's potential and publishes a map, with at least 60 days of public review and comment [S3].

Land near producing wells (within one mile, up to 1,280 acres) can still be leased to prevent drainage of oil from neighboring operations, so genuine production is protected; a variance process with a public-interest determination allows rare exceptions [S2][S3].

The bill explicitly leaves existing multiple-use and environmental review requirements, including the National Environmental Policy Act, fully intact, so it narrows the leasing program without weakening other public-lands safeguards [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose the ability to cheaply acquire and hold speculative leases on land their own industry data show is unlikely to produce. The Bureau of Land Management bears new administrative work to complete and periodically update development analyses with public comment periods.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds process before every lease: completing or updating development scenarios, mapping, and 60-day public comment periods. That takes staff time and could delay leasing even on promising acreage, which supporters of faster domestic production would object to [S3].

Mandatory 15-year updates to development scenarios could leave analyses outdated between cycles, and the drainage and variance exceptions, while narrow, still let some low-potential land be leased [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost is administrative: the Bureau of Land Management must do more analysis and public outreach before leasing, which slows some sales. The benefit is that public land with little or no oil potential stops being locked up by cheap speculative leases that produce almost nothing for taxpayers and block grazing, recreation, and conservation uses. The exceptions for land near producing wells keep genuine drilling largely unaffected, so the tradeoff favors the public unless leasing delays on productive land become significant.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which never scheduled it for a hearing, markup, or floor vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Susie Lee (D-NV) introduced the bill on May 16, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1][S5].
Six House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on [S4].
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no committee markup, no report, no floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies keep the status quo: they can continue acquiring cheap speculative leases on low-potential federal land, and the public keeps footing the administrative cost and losing the other uses of that land.

for.name: Rep. Susie Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it into the House Natural Resources Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill saw no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill sat in a committee controlled by House Republicans without ever advancing.

industries.note: The bill removes their ability to buy cheap leases on land with little or no oil and gas potential, which the bill's findings say rarely produces and yields minimal taxpayer revenue. Genuine production near existing wells is still allowed through drainage and variance exceptions [S2][S3].
Leases on low-potential land can block grazing, recreation, and wildlife uses; ending speculative leasing keeps that land available for other multiple uses at no cost to the public [S3].

The bill's findings state that leases on no- or low-potential land limit the Secretary's ability to support grazing and other multiple-use values, so freeing that land benefits grazing permit holders [S3].
